steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on learning bimanual pinch-grasp skills from a few real-world demonstrations using tactile sensing. Motivate tactile sensing for dexterous manipulation, review optical tactile sensors and learning from demonstration, and end with a contribution subsection.

  - complex, non-trivial deformation of soft sensors during grasping = challenge
  - humans: handle soft contacts, adapt quickly, dual-arm coordination
  - LfD: intuitive, efficient; synchronized tactile info, state-action mapping, sensorimotor skills
  - real-time tactile feedback addresses error accumulation in contact-rich LfD
  - challenge: fuse high-dim tactile data with proprioception for sample-efficient learning

  - framework for bimanual dexterous sensorimotor skills; behavior cloning (BC) from teleoperated demos

  - validated: pinch grasp, dual-arm setup with TacTips (cite); retrieves small cylindrical object from table, few-shot
  - generalizes to unseen objects: diameters, masses, materials
  - robust to external disturbance; autonomous re-grasping after large push-off force

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Dexterous robot manipulation can work across a range of tasks and environments. But enabling dexterous manipulation in robots, especially in a way that is comparable to what humans can do, is still an unsolved challenge. At the moment, many studies use visual feedback so that robots can do dexterous manipulation tasks like box flipping, object rotating, and door opening. But these vision-based methods have limitations, because the visual data can be affected by occlusion and lighting variations. So it is very important to study how tactile information can be incorporated to improve dexterous manipulation in robotic systems.

Tactile sensing plays a vital role in capturing detailed information about contact surfaces, like how the contact forces are distributed and how they vary during force-sensitive tasks, and this is indispensable for dexterous handling of lightweight objects with irregular surfaces, shapes, and deformable properties. Especially during close-range interaction between hands and objects, visual occlusion limits how much detailed information about the contact surfaces can be perceived, and then tactile sensors are valuable because they provide essential information about these surfaces that can't be seen. If tactile sensing is integrated into motor learning of dexterous grasping, it can improve the rich and precise sensing of surface contacts and interaction dynamics, give irreplaceable and direct feedback when objects are manipulated, and allow more robust and precise manipulation tasks. It is crucial to explore how robots can use this information to get dexterous manipulation abilities.

The canonical hardware for robot manipulation has Force/Torque sensors, which can only measure the 6-degree-of-freedom (DoF) wrench at each end-effector. Soft optical-based tactile sensors use a camera system to quantify the deformation of the soft materials, and so they can provide abundant and discriminative contact information. Several soft tactile sensors have been developed so far, including TacTip, DigiTac, Gelsight, and DIGIT. But how to use the high-dimensional data from tactile sensors for contact-rich robot tasks is still open research.

- Learning from Demonstration (LfD)
  - complex, non-trivial deformation of soft sensors during grasping = challenge
  - humans: handle soft contacts, adapt quickly, dual-arm coordination
  - LfD: intuitive, efficient; synchronized tactile info, rich state-action mapping, learn sensorimotor skills
  - real-time tactile feedback addresses error accumulation in contact-rich LfD
  - challenge: fuse high-dim data with proprioceptive states for sample-efficient learning

## I-A Contribution

- framework for bimanual dexterous sensorimotor skills; behavior cloning (BC) from teleoperated demos
- convolutional autoencoder (CAE), self-supervised, extracts tactile features; fused with proprioceptive state
- validated: pinch grasp, dual-arm setup with TacTips; retrieves small cylindrical object from table, few-shot
- generalizes to unseen objects: diameters, masses, materials
- robust to external disturbance; autonomous re-grasping after large push-off force
- saliency map analysis: modality use varies over grasp; segments long-horizon data into fine-skills

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Dexterous robot manipulation can work across a range of tasks and environments. But enabling dexterous manipulation in robots, especially in a way that is comparable to what humans can do, is still an unsolved challenge. At the moment, many studies use visual feedback so that robots can do dexterous manipulation tasks like box flipping, object rotating, and door opening. But these vision-based methods have limitations, because the visual data can be affected by occlusion and lighting variations. So it is very important to study how tactile information can be incorporated to improve dexterous manipulation in robotic systems.

Tactile sensing plays a vital role in capturing detailed information about contact surfaces, like how the contact forces are distributed and how they vary during force-sensitive tasks, and this is indispensable for dexterous handling of lightweight objects with irregular surfaces, shapes, and deformable properties. Especially during close-range interaction between hands and objects, visual occlusion limits how much detailed information about the contact surfaces can be perceived, and then tactile sensors are valuable because they provide essential information about these surfaces that can't be seen. If tactile sensing is integrated into motor learning of dexterous grasping, it can improve the rich and precise sensing of surface contacts and interaction dynamics, give irreplaceable and direct feedback when objects are manipulated, and allow more robust and precise manipulation tasks. It is crucial to explore how robots can use this information to get dexterous manipulation abilities.

The canonical hardware for robot manipulation has Force/Torque sensors, which can only measure the 6-degree-of-freedom (DoF) wrench at each end-effector. Soft optical-based tactile sensors use a camera system to quantify the deformation of the soft materials, and so they can provide abundant and discriminative contact information. Several soft tactile sensors have been developed so far, including TacTip, DigiTac, Gelsight, and DIGIT. But how to use the high-dimensional data from tactile sensors for contact-rich robot tasks is still open research.

The deformation of soft tactile sensors during dexterous grasping tasks is complex and non-trivial, and this is a considerable challenge. Humans can deal with soft contacts, adapt quickly to new tasks, and produce dual-arm coordination skills for manipulating objects. Learning from Demonstration (LfD) is an intuitive and efficient method for acquiring human skills through synchronized tactile information; it encodes rich state-action mapping and lets robots learn human sensorimotor skills while they respond to tactile and proprioceptive feedback. Also, in contact-rich tasks during LfD, errors accumulate because there is no direct feedback, and this can be addressed by incorporating rich tactile feedback in real-time. The challenge is to effectively fuse the high-dimensional data with the robot proprioceptive states so that human dexterous manipulation behavior can be learned in a sample-efficient way.

## I-A Contribution

In this work we present a framework for teaching bimanual, dexterous sensorimotor skills. We use behavior cloning (BC) to learn from human teleoperated demonstrations, to handle the complex dynamics of the deformable tactile sensors. We train a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) in a self-supervised way to extract the essential features from the rich tactile data, and then these features are integrated with the robot's proprioceptive state. With this multimodal fusion the robot can efficiently acquire feedback-driven dexterous grasping skills from a few human demonstrations. We validate the framework with pinch grasp tasks on a dual-arm setup that is equipped with TacTips sensors, and it successfully retrieves a small, cylindrical object on a table using few-shot demonstrations. The experimental results show that the policy learned from few-shot human demonstration data can stably grasp unseen objects with different diameters, masses, and materials.

We also validated that the framework is robust against external disturbances: the learned policy grasps stably under external disturbance, and it can also autonomously re-grasp successfully when a large external force pushes the object off. We used saliency map analysis and showed how the learned policy uses the different sensory modalities in a variable way during the dexterous pinch grasp process. This analysis shows that our proposed network can efficiently use high-dimensional data and autonomously segment the long-horizon data into several distinct fine-skills to execute depending on the contact situation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Dexterous robot manipulation has the capability to work across a range of tasks and environments. However, enabling dexterous manipulation in robots, particularly in a way comparable to human capabilities, remains an unsolved challenge. Currently, numerous studies use visual feedback to enable robots to perform dexterous manipulation tasks such as box flipping [1], object rotating [2], and door opening [3]. However, these vision-based methods have limitations, as the visual data can be influenced by occlusion and lighting variations. Consequently, it is very important to investigate how to incorporate tactile information to enhance dexterous manipulation in robotic systems.

Tactile sensing plays a vital role in capturing detailed information about contact surfaces, including the distribution of contact forces and their variations during force-sensitive tasks, which is indispensable for dexterous handling of lightweight objects with irregular surfaces, shapes, and deformable properties. Especially during close-range interaction between hands and objects, visual occlusion restricts the perception of detailed information about the contact surfaces, and tactile sensors become valuable for providing essential information about these unseeable surfaces. Integrating tactile sensing into motor learning of dexterous grasping can enhance the rich and precise sensing of surface contacts and interaction dynamics, provide irreplaceable and direct feedback when manipulating objects, and enable more robust and precise manipulation [4,5]. It is crucial to explore how robots can leverage this information to achieve dexterous manipulation abilities.

The canonical hardware for robot manipulation incorporates Force/Torque sensors that can only measure the 6-degree-of-freedom (DoF) wrench at each end-effector. Soft optical-based tactile sensors can provide abundant and discriminative contact information by using a camera system to quantify the deformation of the soft materials [5]. Several soft tactile sensors have been developed, including TacTip [6], DigiTac [7], Gelsight [8], and DIGIT [9]. However, how to use the high-dimensional data from tactile sensors for contact-rich robot tasks remains open research.

The complex and non-trivial deformation of soft tactile sensors during dexterous grasping tasks presents a considerable challenge. Humans can deal with soft contacts, quickly adapt to new tasks, and produce dual-arm coordination skills for manipulating objects. Learning from Demonstration (LfD) offers an intuitive, efficient method for acquiring human skills through synchronized tactile information, encoding a rich state-action mapping and enabling robots to learn human sensorimotor skills while responding to tactile and proprioceptive feedback. Additionally, the accumulation of errors in contact-rich tasks during LfD, caused by the lack of direct feedback, can be addressed by incorporating rich tactile feedback in real-time. The challenge lies in effectively fusing high-dimensional data with robot proprioceptive states for sample-efficient learning of human dexterous manipulation behavior.

## I-A Contribution

In this work, we present a framework for teaching bimanual, dexterous sensorimotor skills. To handle the complex dynamics of deformable tactile sensors, we employ behavior cloning (BC) to learn from human teleoperated demonstrations. A convolutional autoencoder (CAE) is trained in a self-supervised manner to extract essential features from the rich tactile data, which are then integrated with the robot's proprioceptive state. This multimodal fusion enables the robot to efficiently acquire feedback-driven dexterous grasping skills from a few human demonstrations. The proposed framework is validated on pinch grasp tasks on a dual-arm setup equipped with TacTips sensors [6] and successfully retrieves a small, cylindrical object on a table using few-shot demonstrations. Our experimental results show that the policy learned from few-shot human demonstration data achieves stable grasping of unseen objects with different diameters, masses, and materials.

Furthermore, we validated the robustness of the framework against external disturbances: the learned policy grasps stably under external disturbance and can autonomously execute a successful re-grasp when a large external force pushes the object off. Using saliency map analysis [10], we revealed how the learned policy uses different sensory modalities in a variable way throughout the dexterous pinch grasp process. This analysis demonstrates that our proposed network can efficiently use high-dimensional data and autonomously segment the long-horizon data into several distinct fine-skills for execution according to different contact situations.
